notice: PROVISIONAL RESEARCH DRAFTS. Each claim was drafted with AI assistance from the cited passages and has NOT been verified by a practitioner. verification_status is 'unverified' for every claim. Quotes must match the extracted source text exactly; the ingestion pipeline rejects any quote it cannot locate. Traditional textual claims are not clinical efficacy claims. Translations quoted from the 1890 Kaviratna edition render Pandu as 'chlorosis' and Kamala as 'anaemia'; these are the translator's choices, not equivalences.

concepts.name: Oleation with medicated ghee (snehana) in Pandu
Purification (saṃśodhana) with sharp emetic and purgative drugs after oleation, in Pandu
Wholesome diet (pathya) after purification, in Pandu
Medication chosen according to the predominant dosha, in Pandu
Old śāli rice, barley and wheat with soups
Soups of mung bean, pigeon pea and lentil
Water boiled with the sthirādi group of drugs, for drinking and cooking
Iron powder macerated in cow's urine, given with milk (ayorajas)

claims.subject: S-PALLOR
claims.statement: The classical texts name Pandu after the pallor (pāṇḍu colour) that predominates among the skin discolourations it produces.

evidence.quote: sarveṣu caiteṣviha pāṇḍubhāvo yato+adhiko+ataḥ khalu pāṇḍurogaḥ

uncertainty: Discolouration may be pale, yellowish or greenish; pallor is the predominant one.

claims.subject: S-PALPITATION
claims.statement: Palpitation is listed among the premonitory signs (pūrvarūpa) of Pandu.

evidence.quote: Palpitation of the heart, dryness of the system, the absence of perspiration, and a sense of fatigue

uncertainty: Premonitory (prodromal) sign rather than a sign of the established disease.

claims.subject: S-DRY-SKIN
claims.statement: Dryness is listed among the premonitory signs of Pandu.
uncertainty: Premonitory sign; the 1890 translation renders it as 'dryness of the system'.

claims.subject: S-ABSENT-SWEATING
claims.statement: Absence of sweating is listed among the premonitory signs of Pandu.
uncertainty: Premonitory sign.

claims.subject: S-FATIGUE
claims.statement: Fatigue (śrama) is listed both as a premonitory sign and as a sign of manifest Pandu.

evidence.quote: and a sense of fatigue (without having undergone any exertion)

claims.subject: S-WEAKNESS
claims.statement: General weakness (daurbalya) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.

claims.subject: S-DIZZINESS
claims.statement: Giddiness (bhrama) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.
uncertainty: Bhrama is translated as giddiness or vertigo; mapping to the modern symptom 'dizziness' needs practitioner confirmation.

claims.subject: S-TINNITUS
claims.statement: Ringing in the ears (karṇakṣveḍa) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.

evidence.quote: the appearance of a rumbling noise in his ears

claims.subject: S-ANOREXIA
claims.statement: Aversion to food is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.

evidence.quote: of the body, disrelish for food, a sense of the body being pressed down

claims.subject: S-BREATHLESSNESS
claims.statement: Breathlessness (śvāsa) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.
uncertainty: The 1890 translation renders śvāsa as 'asthmatic breathing'.

claims.subject: S-FEVER
claims.statement: Fever is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.

claims.subject: S-BODY-ACHE
claims.statement: Pain in the limbs (gātraśūla) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.

claims.subject: S-PERIORBITAL-SWELLING
claims.statement: Swelling around the eyes (śūnākṣikūṭa) is listed among the signs of manifest Pandu.
uncertainty: Akṣikūṭa denotes the orbital region; the 1890 translation renders it as 'eye-balls'.

claims.subject: R-PANDU
claims.statement: In Pandu the vitiated doshas are described as pitta-predominant.
uncertainty: Pitta predominance applies to Pandu in general; vātaja and kaphaja types are also described.

claims.subject: R-PANDU

uncertainty: Purification procedures (emesis, purgation) require clinical supervision; this is a classical principle, not a self-care instruction.

reference_evidence.quote: The most important promoters of iron absorption in foods are ascorbic acid, lactic acid (produced by fermentation), meat factors in animal meat, the presence of heme iron, and alcohol which stimulate iron uptake by inhibition of hepcidin expression.
uncertainty: Mechanistic review statement; alcohol is listed as a promoter of absorption, not as advice.

reference_evidence.quote: The most important inhibitors of iron uptake are phytic acid/phytates, polyphenols/tannins, proteins from soya beans, milk, eggs, and calcium.

Heme iron, which is ferrous iron present in haemoglobin in the red blood cells and myoglobin in the myocytes, is absorbed within the intact protoporphyrin molecule threefold to fourfold more efficiently than inorganic ferric iron.
concluded that “vitamin C contributes to increasing nonheme iron absorption”
uncertainty: The review notes the effect is less pronounced in complete diets than in single-meal studies.

It can be caused by a reduced dietary intake of iron or increased need, acute or chronic blood loss, and intestinal malabsorption of iron

The classic laboratory findings of iron deficiency anemia include a decrease in the hemoglobin (Hb) level, serum iron concentration, serum transferrin saturation, and serum ferritin level, and an increase in total iron-binding capacity.
Oral iron therapy is given as the first-line treatment for IDA.
uncertainty: Review focused on pregnancy and the postpartum period.

known_gaps: No explicit lifestyle recommendation was found in the Pandu chapters read (Caraka Ci.16, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya Ni.13, Suśruta Utt.44). The causes listed in Ca.6.16.8 (day sleep, exercise and sexual activity during indigestion, suppression of urges) are not converted into lifestyle recommendations, because that would be an inference.

Dietary avoidances (e.g. Ca.6.16.84: avoid kulattha, kākamācī, kapota with Yogarāja) cannot be expressed: the ontology has no avoidance or contraindication predicate. Contraindications belong to Component 3.
No Sinhala-language source; Sinhala terms are not included.
Botanical names are recorded only as stated by the 1890 translation and are not taxonomically verified.
Halīmaka and Kāmalā (related conditions) are not modelled as separate Roga claims in this version.
Modern reference evidence concerns iron-deficiency anaemia; it is not equivalent to Pandu and is not linked to Pandu claims except as an explicit qualification.
